messages.subject: proposal draft for RStan interface
parts:
Ahead of working on the Python/R under-the-hood refactor when
Allen gets here, I tried to go through the current R interface and
whittle things down (and expand a bit) to where I think it should go.
I'd think that roughly the same interface would work in Python.

I hope this is close enough to idiomatic for R that it's not
too embarrassing --- but please send feedback (up to and including
telling me I should just stay out of R!).

The biggest change is simplifying what functions do and where some
of the action is, as well as splitting some of the functions out (like
stan() is now stan_nuts, stan_hmc, and stan_diagnose).

I don't think this loses any functionality other than the big fit
object, which I don't think we should have. And it's assuming some
functionality we don't yet have, like being able to input a mass matrix.

I can move this over to a wiki (on RStan or Stan's repo?) if people
think that'll be easier and the response isn't to just get out of the
way of RStan.

- Bob


1. Compilation
------------------------------------------------------------
The compilation function compiles a Stan program to a dynamic shared
object (DSO) and optionally saves it.

compiled_program
rtan::stan_compile( # DEFAULTS
source = (<string> || <path>) # no default
name = <string>, # empty
boost = <path>, # use BH
eigen = <path>, # use RcppEigen
opt = ("fast" || "debug"), # "fast"
save_dso = <bool>, # FALSE
debug_code = <bool> # TRUE
);

* Is there any reason to keep the name option?
* How long-lived is the "save_dso" option?
- Where is it saved?
* If we allow optimize settings, is there a way to have it scope
over just the call and not affect the R global build environment?
* Is there a way we can have make-like behavior here where if there's
a saved version and the model file or code have not changed, don't
do anything?
* Do we need the other existing compiler options ("presentation1",
"presentation2", and "small")?
* Should the save_dso provide a path rather than a boolean?
* Is it possible to save the DSO across sessions?
* Should the dave_dso defalt be true and if so, use temp?
* Do we ever need NDEBUG=false? That is, shouldn't we just always
have -DNDEBUG set to turn off debugging? (The double-negative

compiled_program
--------------------
This should only include the compiled Stan program and methods
to do variable conversion, extract names, compute log densities, etc.

Slots:
name : <string>
stan_code : <string>
cpp_code : <string>
dso : <S4 cxxdso> (from inline)
cxx_flags: <string>

jacobian = <bool>);

return$grad : <vector>

* Seems there should be a better way to organize this, but I
can't see it. And maybe some shorter names


2. NUTS
------------------------------------------------------------

mcmc_fit
rstan::stan_nuts(
program = <compiled_program>, # no default
data = (<list> || <environment>), # top-level environment by default
max_treedepth = <int>, # 10
chain_ids = <ints>, # 1:4
num_warmup = <int>, # 10
num_samples = <int>, # 10
init=(<double> # 2.0
|| <list>
|| <list of lists>
|| <function>)
stepsize=<double>, # 1.0
metric = ("unit_e", # "diag_e"
|| "diag_e"
|| "dense_e"
|| <vector>
|| <matrix>),
adapt_stepsize = <bool>, # TRUE
adapt_mass_matrix = <bool>, # TRUE
adapt = list(gamma=<double>,
kappa=<double>,
t0=<double>,
init_buffer=<int>,
term_buffer=<int>,
adapt_window=<int>) # ...
params_to_save = (NA
|| <vector(char)>) # NA
save_warmup = <bool>, # TRUE
thin = <int>, # 1
sample_file = <path>, # NA
diagnostic_file = <path>, # NA
refresh = <int>, # 1

|| "standard"
|| "verbose"), # standard

* Return value just includes the result in such a way that it
can be extracted as before.
* Return value won't include the compiled program (or source).
* Should return value include timing information?
* There's no append_samples = <bool>
* There's no option to compile the model from within the stan_nuts
call.
* data defaults to top-level environment with lazy read (not how
it's done now); list is list of values as before
* Instead of "chains" and a start ID, there's just a "chain_ids"
argument supplying both the chains and the ID, defaulting to the usual
* Default num_warmup and num_samples very small by default (but shouldn't
be so small as to trigger scary messages about adaptation)
* Metric is specified by name of type or by value; the names default
to unit values for init
* Those adapt parameters are all for adapt_stepsize, right?
* Are there adaptation parameters for mass_matrix, like regularization?
* params_to_save defaults to NA (or all), or a positive list of whole
parameter names.
* sample_file gets a copy of the output written to it, but return
object still created --- should this just move so that the return
object has a save on it? Or should setting this cause the return of

------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------

So my big problem with this flat structure is a conceptual one.
Right now there’s a glut of terrible algorithm names out there
because people don’t understand the foundations of HMC.
Consequently "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo” is often relegated
to what is more properly called Metropolis-Corrected Euclidean
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a static integration time, and
every tweak yields a new name. This flurry of names obfuscates
the real underlying mathematical framework — changing the
metric doesn’t really lead to a new algorithm, just a different
implementation. Why, for example, would RHMC receive
its own command but EHMC with a diagonal metric vs EHMC
with a dense metric would be different options within the same
command? Moreover, a single command “stan_hmc” that
just calls one of this configurations makes everything so much
worse.

At the very least we need to be more careful with the names.
I know we all love NUTS, but it’s really just an implementation
of a more general idea of dynamic integration time (really the
no-U-turn part of it is the least novel — the really important
part of the algorithm is binary tree to preserve reversibility).
What we have are two main different configuration options:

Metric: Identity, diagonal Euclidean, dense Euclidean (and in the future SoftAbs Riemannian)
Integration Time: Static vs Exhaustive (i.e. integrate longer on bigger level sets, NUTS is an example)

Why is integration time a better split than metric?

Then there’s the fact that we can sample or optimize, and
the current names make no distinction between the two
If people are that against hierarchical arguments (note
that we have yet to have any complaint from users on
the list — the CmdStan user base is small, but it’s not
negligible) then we at least have to maintain the hierarchy
is the command names: stan_mcmc_*, stan_opt_*, stan_vb_*, etc.

Finally, maintaining this orgy of commands is going to be a
pain in the ass. What to change one argument that all of the
commands share? Go ahead and tweak every single command
config.

On 06/01, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> So my big problem with this flat structure is a conceptual one.
> Right now there’s a glut of terrible algorithm names out there
> because people don’t understand the foundations of HMC.
> Consequently "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo” is often relegated
> to what is more properly called Metropolis-Corrected Euclidean
> Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a static integration time, and
> every tweak yields a new name. This flurry of names obfuscates
> the real underlying mathematical framework — changing the
> metric doesn’t really lead to a new algorithm, just a different
> implementation. Why, for example, would RHMC receive
> its own command but EHMC with a diagonal metric vs EHMC
> with a dense metric would be different options within the same
> command? Moreover, a single command “stan_hmc” that
> just calls one of this configurations makes everything so much
> worse.
>
> At the very least we need to be more careful with the names.
> I know we all love NUTS, but it’s really just an implementation
> of a more general idea of dynamic integration time (really the
> no-U-turn part of it is the least novel — the really important
> part of the algorithm is binary tree to preserve reversibility).
> What we have are two main different configuration options:
>
> Metric: Identity, diagonal Euclidean, dense Euclidean (and in the future SoftAbs Riemannian)
> Integration Time: Static vs Exhaustive (i.e. integrate longer on bigger level sets, NUTS is an example)
>
> Why is integration time a better split than metric?
>

These are good points. And they relate to the design of the "config
object" as well as the organization of a family of functions.

> Then there’s the fact that we can sample or optimize, and
> the current names make no distinction between the two
> If people are that against hierarchical arguments (note
> that we have yet to have any complaint from users on
> the list — the CmdStan user base is small, but it’s not
> negligible) then we at least have to maintain the hierarchy
> is the command names: stan_mcmc_*, stan_opt_*, stan_vb_*, etc.
>
> Finally, maintaining this orgy of commands is going to be a
> pain in the ass. What to change one argument that all of the
> commands share? Go ahead and tweak every single command
> config.
>

I agree that maintaining this multitude of commands is going to be a
pain in the ass. I think it will be *slightly* easier than the status
quo, which requires a giant switch statement depending on the algorithm
to do the same thing.

More concretely: I've been bitten once by a typo in handling/"parsing"
the unwieldy config object (same config object in RStan and PyStan) and
I think using functions would make those kinds of errors much easier to
spot.

Bref, I don't see how it will make things worse and it might make things
better.


Thanks,

Allen

I have sympathy --- my problem with the hiearchical structure
is a conceptual one, too.

There are two things I'm suggesting doing differently:

* flattening arguments
* separating top-level commands

My main motivation is to simplify the functions from
the user's perspective by removing argument interactions and
making the functions or command-line invocations more idiomatic.
And also make backward compatibility easier.

So the reason plain-old Euclidean HMC is split from
NUTS is that they take two conflicting config params
(integration time and max depth; whereas the metric is just
a free choice).

The downside is that it increases the number of functions.
This would be bad if a lot of them were used and you had
to constantly choose which one to use.

I can live with stan_mcmc_... and stan_opt_...

I think the full set of top-level commands now would be:

SHORT LONG

stan_lbfgs stan_opt_lbfgs
stan_bfgs stan_opt_bfgs

stan_hmc stan_mcmc_hmc_static
stan_nuts stan_mcmc_hmc_nuts

stan_diagnose stan_diagnose

I think the following are in our short-term future:

stan_bbvb stan_approx_bbvb

stan_rhmc stan_mcmc_hmc_static_riemannian
stan_geonuts stan_mcmc_hmc_nuts_riemannian

and maybe

stan_stochastic_bbvb stan_approx_stochastic_bbvb

stan_mml stan_opt_mml

I'm particularly worried about backward compatibility in
the hierarchical formulation.

I think Andrew/Ben/Rob want to include something to parse
the lme4/glm syntax to implement somehting like:

stan_glm ???
stan_lme ???

- Bob

I am warning everyone that I will fight this hard. If we want to
abstract to a default then just go with stan_sample or stan_mcmc.
stan_hmc just reinforces this false idea that people have that
HMC is just Euclidean HMC with a static integration time and
every other config is some fancy new algorithm. But it’s not —
HMC is a very general construction and we need to emphasize
this so that people understand we’re just not offering a new
heuristic algorithm but an entirely new perspective of MCMC.

>> stan_mcmc_ehmc_exhaustive
>
> Why "exhaustive" for NUTS?

It’s what were calling a new class of algorithms with dynamic
integration times (as in the integration time expands until
the trajectory “exhausts” exploration on the level set). NUTS
is an example — the binary tree to preserve detailed balance
will be a general element of these methods, although the NUTS
criterion itself may likely change to something more theoretically
motivated.

> And you don't see commands in languages like R that say things like:
>
> mypackagename_linear_regression_nonheteroscedastic_normal_noise(...)
>
> you see commands like lm(), where the lack of "g" means it's plain
> old linear regression and the normal noise is taken for granted.

And people also use “Metropolis” to refer to Random Walk Metropolis
with an isotropic Gaussian proposal, which causes no end of confusion.
For example, I keep hearing “Metropolis is random walk, so all Metropolis
algorithms are bad, right?” which confuses the hell out of people when
you try to respond with HMC being implemented with a Metropolis correction
in practice. Notation and conventions are terrible in statistical software and
that’s no excuse for us to use poor names, too.

Again, if you want to have a default sampling config fine. But don’t make
a default HMC config and call it “stan_hmc” or we’ll be digging out of that
convention for a long, long time.

If we make the various configs into formal classes, we can just have the sampling() (or whatever we rename it to) dispatch on the config object in addition to the model object). Then we wouldn't have a proliferation of function names, just a proliferation of class names for the config objects.

I quickly reimplemented the current configuration as S4 classes in R (attached). After a source(), you could do
new("stan_hmc")
or whatever to instantiate an object that has the defaults for HMC. This retains the hierarchical structure of CmdStan calls, validates the input, doesn't have slots that are inapplicable given other options, and does not require us to write too many functions that are callable by the user. Ben

The reason to make classes immutable is that it's easier to
guarantee they're always in safe and usable states. And it
automatically makes them threadsafe, which would otherwise require
synchronization on the gets/sets.

It's often hard to do with getters/setters if you have linked
states to get and set. For instance, if you have a class

struct {
real l_;
real u_;
}

with a constraint that l_ < u_, then you can't update that without
setting l_ and u_ at the same time because they're not independent
in validation. The more interactions, the harder the getter/setter
design (and the harder the validation in general).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
parts:
Right, but a hierarchical config wouldn’t have any interactions
per say.  You could modify NUTS parameters even if NUTS
wasn’t the active HMC implementation.  In other words, you
have a big ol’ tree of parameters and the mutators would
ensure that each node has a valid value (validity being
defined by each parameter definition) and then at runtime
the config gets executed and selects out a single subtree
of active parameters.  Because the global tree is valid
each subtree will be valid.

Anyways, I’m just saying that a global config object
would be easy to manipulate safely.  It doesn’t get
around the overhead for learning a hierarchical
structure.  Also, there’s the interface consistency.
I think if we went with something like this we’d
have to not use methods but rather have functions
that take in a config class,

stan_config
stan_config.hmc.stepsize.set(0.0001)
sample(stan_config)

which would then roughly parallel the CmdStan
execution of 

./model sample stan_config_string

The reason to make classes immutable is that it's easier to
guarantee they're always in safe and usable states.  And it
automatically makes them threadsafe, which would otherwise require
synchronization on the gets/sets.  

It's often hard to do with getters/setters if you have linked
states to get and set.  For instance, if you have a class

 struct {
   real l_;
   real u_;
 }

with a constraint that l_ < u_, then you can't update that without
setting l_ and u_ at the same time because they're not independent
in validation.  The more interactions, the harder the getter/setter
design (and the harder the validation in general).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
parts:
Are you proposing changing the defaults of num_warmup and num_samples (1000 each)? If so, then we should do that for all the interfaces.

Yes, I think we agreed on 100 for all the interfaces.
We should make sure everyone agrees.  Too many people turn on 2000 and

then go away for the weekend.

I think 100 might be too small.  It might be fine for social science models
but for complex likelihoods (especially with ODEs) the adaptation typically
needs longer than 100.  I’d suggest 250 minimum, with a warning to users
that they might need more if they’re seeing poor sampling.

Looks like Michael strongly agrees with this.  We absolutely
have to get Michael's approval on whatever we call anything that
smacks of "HMC".  I'm very confused as to why Michael thinks
everyone's confused, but that's the nature of confusion.

Once again, the problem is that people currently equate “Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo” with what should more formally be called “Metropolis-corrected 
Euclidean Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with static integration time”.  So when
you tweak any of those properties people think it’s a different algorithm
and we lose the concept of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo being this very
general approach.  This is a ubiquitous problem in MCMC  as it also
happens with Metropolis-Hastings (people confusing the general 
Metropolis-Hastings construction vs particular proposals).

I want the naming to emphasize that any default is just _an_ implementation
of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo not _the_ implementation of Hamiltonian Monte
Carlo.  Having a “stan_hmc” option does the latter.

parts:
We might keep in mind that we can probably accommodate some differences
between interfaces. For example, on `sample_file` I don't know of a
Python package that both returns values and writes out the same values
to a csv file in the same step (esp. in a world that's moving away from
CSV files and towards things like JSON and HDF5), but it probably
doesn't matter if one interface does something slightly different here.

This is another thing that changes in the writer refactor as all
sample output gets passed to the interfaces piece by piece
by the callbacks.

But this does raise an important issue — in the new refactored
architecture each interface will be responsible for creating
writers and var_contexts which may or may not require their
own arguments.  So we can’t talk about a single config object
in isolation, rather we’ll have “internal” arguments and “interface”
arguments and we should keep this dichotomy in mind.
